To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the antennular flagellums of crayfish are sensitive to both hydrodynamic and chemical cues; (2) the flagellum is a sensory organ for both types of stimuli; (3) there is directional asymmetry in the response of local interneuron Type I to hydrodynamic stimulation, but not to chemical stimulation; (4) this response asymmetry is consistent with the asymmetry in the flow field of the flagellum during antennular flicking; and (5)

the responses of crayfish deutocerbral Type I local interneurons to hydrodynamic stimulation are directionally asymmetric, and that this directional asymmetry can be explained in terms of the asymmetries of hydrodynamic flow past the beaked hairs of the lateral antennule.

the response of a local interneuron in the deutocerebral antennular neuropil to hydrodynamic stimulation depends on the direction of fluid movement past the flagellar beaked hairs, but does not depend on the direction of movement of the flagellar odorant receptors.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the sensory basis for antennular flicking, and the role of the antennular flagellums in the crayfish's detection of hydrodynamic stimuli.
the role of antennular flagellar receptors in the crayfish olfactory system.
the role of hydrodynamic flow asymmetry in antennular behavior and in the processing of hydrodynamic information.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, in the crayfish, there exists a directional asymmetry in the response of local interneurones in the deutocerebrun to hydrodynamic flow past the lateral flagellum.
Type I interneurons are bimodally (hydrodynamic and chemosensory) sensitive and that the hydrodynamic sensitivity is direction-dependent.
the antennal flagellum is not only an organ for the detection of water-borne odorant molecules but also a hydrodynamic flow sensor.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Type I neurons are sensitive to the direction of abrupt hydrodynamic stimuli, but not to the direction of odorant stimuli.
the Type I local interneurons are not directionally selective with regard to the flow direction of odorants, but they are directionally selective with respect to hydrodynamic flow direction.
the Type I interneurons respond more vigorously when the flow direction is proximal→distral than in the opposite flow direction.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the crayfish deutoccerebrum contains local interneurons that are bimodally responsive to odorant and hydrodynamic stimuli, and that the responses of these neurons to hydrodynamic stimulation are asymmetric.
the Type I neurons are sensitive to the direction of water flow past the lateral antennule, but that they do not respond to the same flow direction with the same magnitude.

, in the crayfish, hydrodynamic stimulation of a lateral antennular flagellar sensory field can produce directional asymmetry in responses from local interneurons, which may be of behavioral relevance.
